name: Adam Osborne
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; earned BSc in chemical engineering in 1961 and was pursuing graduate studies at the University of Delaware. Founded Osborne and Associates (computer book publishing) in 1972 at age 33 and launched the Osborne 1 portable computer in 1981 at age 42.
early_history_summary: Born in Bangkok to British parents, spent childhood in India, moved to England at age 11. Graduated from University of Birmingham in 1961 with a chemical engineering degree, then moved to the US for graduate studies, completing his PhD at the University of Delaware in 1968.
family_context_summary: Born to British parents in Bangkok; father Arthur Osborne was a university lecturer and devotee of Eastern religion who moved the family to an ashram in India. Mother Lucia was a homemaker.
evidence_summary: Osborne's entrepreneurial achievements came well after age 26. By 26 he was a graduate student in chemical engineering with no notable milestone in computing or business. His computer industry fame arrived with the Osborne 1 in 1981 at age 42.

name: Regla Torres
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold medal at the 1991 Pan American Games with Cuba at age 16, then became the youngest Olympic volleyball champion in history at age 17 at the 1992 Barcelona Games.
early_history_summary: Torres started playing volleyball at age 8 in Havana after teachers noticed her exceptional height. She entered a sports school in the fourth grade, joined the national team at age 14, and rapidly developed into a dominant middle blocker on the Cuban national team.
family_context_summary: Born in Havana to separated parents; mother raised her and insisted she pursue volleyball over high jump. Father remained involved in upbringing despite separation. Family was not affluent; mother placed her in sports school partly out of childcare necessity.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; mother chose volleyball for Torres but had no domain expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cuban sports school system, exceptional height, early specialization, national team at 14
evidence_summary: Torres was identified early for her exceptional height (1.91m) and channeled into Cuba's state sports school system from the fourth grade. She joined the national team at 14 and won Pan American Games gold at 16 and Olympic gold at 17. The Cuban volleyball pipeline provided elite coaching, facilities, and competition density. Her parents' separation created the practical need for sports school placement, which became the entry point to her career.
starting_point: Born in Havana, Cuba to a modest family; parents separated during her childhood, mother raised her and worked, placing Torres in sports school partly out of childcare necessity.
current_position: Former volleyball legend working as a coach; joined Uralochka-NTMK coaching staff in Russia and directed a team in Mexico's professional league; stepped away from Cuban volleyball administration in 2023 citing decline.

trajectory.event: Won gold medal at the Pan American Games in Havana, her first major international title.
Became the youngest Olympic volleyball champion in history at the Barcelona Games.
Won FIVB World Championship in Brazil and was named tournament MVP.
Won second Olympic gold medal at the Atlanta Games.
Won third consecutive Olympic gold medal at the Sydney Games.
Named Best Female Player of the 20th Century by the FIVB and inducted into the International Volleyball Hall of Fame.

name: Georgina Rizk
milestone_by_age_26: Crowned Miss Universe 1971 at age 18, becoming the first Lebanese and first Arab woman to win the title.
early_history_summary: Rizk was born in Beirut and began modeling at age 14 after being discovered by model Andrée Lavidiotti, who mentored her with strict diet and training. She won Miss Lebanon 1970, competed at Miss World 1970 (unplaced), then won Miss Universe 1971 in Miami.
family_context_summary: Born in Beirut to a Lebanese father who worked in the customs department and a Hungarian mother described as a baroness. Had an admiring sister and attended Holy Family School for 12 years.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no family connection to modeling or pageants.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Natural beauty, early modeling mentor, pageant system
evidence_summary: Rizk's Miss Universe win at 18 was driven primarily by her natural physical beauty, which was noticed at age 14 by model Andrée Lavidiotti. Lavidiotti mentored her with strict diet, posture training, and modeling development. Her mixed Lebanese-Hungarian heritage contributed to a distinctive appearance. She had no family connections to the pageant or modeling world; her entry came through being spotted at a young age.
starting_point: Born in Beirut, Lebanon to a Lebanese customs official father and a Hungarian mother described as a baroness; middle-class family with no connections to entertainment or pageants.
current_position: Living in Lebanon; married to Lebanese singer Walid Toufic since 1990; remains the only Arab woman to have won Miss Universe.

trajectory.event: Won Miss Lebanon title and competed at Miss World 1970 (unplaced).
Crowned Miss Universe in Miami, becoming the first Lebanese and first Arab woman to win the title.
Married Ali Hassan Salameh, a leading figure in the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Salameh was killed in a car bomb in Beirut; Rizk was pregnant with their son Ali at the time.
Remarried Lebanese singer Walid Toufic; they have two children together.

name: Daniel Narcisse
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2001 World Championship with France and the French Championship with Chambéry Savoie at age 21, establishing himself as one of the most decorated French handball players.
early_history_summary: Narcisse started playing handball at Joinville on Réunion island and joined Chambéry Savoie Handball in 1998 at age 18. He made his French national team debut in 2000 and won his first World Championship title in 2001 at age 21.
family_context_summary: Born in Saint-Denis, Réunion, an overseas department of France. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Early handball in Réunion, move to mainland France, physical talent, national team
evidence_summary: Narcisse developed his handball skills from youth on Réunion island before moving to mainland France to join Chambéry at 18. His exceptional vertical leap earned him the nickname 'Air France.' The French national team system provided the platform for his World Championship win at 21. Coming from an overseas department required geographic relocation to access elite competition, a mild form of adversity that shaped his path.
starting_point: Born in Saint-Denis, Réunion (French overseas department); family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from professional handball in 2018 after five years with Paris Saint-Germain; widely regarded as one of the most decorated French handball players with nine international titles.

trajectory.event: Won World Championship with France and French Championship with Chambéry Savoie.
Won Olympic gold medal at the Beijing Games and was named All-star left back.
Won EHF Champions League with THW Kiel in his first season at the club.
Won second Olympic gold at London and was named IHF World Player of the Year.
Retired from professional handball after five years with Paris Saint-Germain.

name: Marek Janowski
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; by 1965 he was working as a young conductor in Düsseldorf with early conducting opportunities. His first music director appointment was in Freiburg in 1973 at age 34.
early_history_summary: Born in Warsaw, grew up in Wuppertal, Germany after his mother fled during World War II. Studied music in Germany and worked as a répétiteur in Aachen and Cologne before gaining conducting opportunities in Düsseldorf from 1964.
family_context_summary: Born in Warsaw; father disappeared in Poland during World War II. Mother traveled to Wuppertal, Germany to be with her parents. Grew up as a Polish-German war child in Nazi Germany.
evidence_summary: Janowski's conducting career followed the traditional German Kapellmeister path with early assistant positions. By age 26 he was gaining conducting experience in Düsseldorf but had not achieved a material milestone. His reputation grew with music director appointments in Freiburg (1973) and Dortmund (1975), well after age 26.

name: Teófilo Stevenson
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in heavyweight boxing at the 1972 Munich Games at age 20, having previously won bronze at the 1971 Pan American Games at age 19.
early_history_summary: Stevenson began boxing at age 9 under former national light heavyweight champion John Herrera at a makeshift open-air gym in Puerto Padre, Cuba. He won a junior title and was brought into Cuba's state sports system, making his international debut at the 1971 Pan American Games and winning Olympic gold in 1972.
family_context_summary: Born in Puerto Padre, Cuba to Teófilo Stevenson Patterson, an immigrant from Saint Vincent who gave English lessons and boxed seven fights, and Dolores Lawrence, a native Cuban whose parents immigrated from Saint Kitts. Modest working-class family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father had brief boxing experience (seven fights) and encouraged Teófilo's interest in the sport, though he was not a professional boxer. Father accompanied him to early fights.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cuban state boxing system, father's boxing background, John Herrera mentorship, exceptional physical power
evidence_summary: Stevenson's path was shaped by Cuba's post-revolutionary state sports system, which identified and developed boxing talent through state academies. His father's brief boxing experience provided initial familiarity with the sport. Crucially, former national light heavyweight champion John Herrera trained him from age 9 at a local gym. Stevenson's exceptional size (6'3") and power were evident early, and the Cuban system accelerated him to international competition by age 19 and Olympic gold by 20.
starting_point: Born in Puerto Padre, Cuba to a modest working-class family; father was an immigrant from Saint Vincent who gave English lessons and had brief boxing experience, mother was of Caribbean immigrant descent.
current_position: Died June 11, 2012 in Havana at age 60; remembered as one of the greatest amateur boxers in history with three Olympic gold medals and three world amateur championships.

trajectory.event: Won bronze at the Pan American Games in Cali, his first major international medal.
Won Olympic gold medal in heavyweight boxing at the Munich Games.
Won world amateur championship in Havana.
Won second Olympic gold medal at the Montreal Games.
Won third Olympic gold medal at the Moscow Games.
Won third world amateur championship in Reno at age 36.
Died in Havana on June 11, 2012.

name: Zbigniew Boniek
milestone_by_age_26: Played in the 1978 FIFA World Cup at age 22 and was named Polish Footballer of the Year; won Polish league championships with Widzew Łódź in 1981 and 1982 before transferring to Juventus.
early_history_summary: Boniek began his youth career at Zawisza Bydgoszcz in 1966 at age 10, debuted for the senior team in 1973 at 17, and moved to Widzew Łódź in 1975 at 19. He made his Poland national team debut in 1976 and starred at the 1978 World Cup, earning Polish Footballer of the Year honors.
family_context_summary: Born in Bydgoszcz, Poland. Family background not documented in reviewed sources beyond birthplace.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Youth academy at Zawisza, early senior debut at 17, Polish football system, communist-era constraints
evidence_summary: Boniek's path was built on early immersion in Polish football, joining Zawisza Bydgoszcz's youth system at 10 and debuting professionally at 17. His move to Widzew Łódź at 19 and national team debut at 20 positioned him for the 1978 World Cup breakthrough. Growing up in communist Poland provided limited resources but a structured football pipeline. His talent was recognized early but no specific family advantages or elite mentorship are documented.
starting_point: Born in Bydgoszcz, Poland; family background not documented in reviewed sources. Grew up in communist-era Poland with limited economic resources.
current_position: Former UEFA vice-president (2021-2025) and former president of the Polish Football Federation (2012-2021); considered one of the greatest Polish footballers of all time.

trajectory.event: Played in the 1978 FIFA World Cup and was named Polish Footballer of the Year.
Won Polish league championship with Widzew Łódź.
Won second Polish league title; led Poland to World Cup bronze with a hat-trick against Belgium; transferred to Juventus for a record Polish fee.
Won European Cup Winners' Cup and European Super Cup with Juventus.
Won European Cup with Juventus, the club's first.
Named to Pelé's FIFA 100 list of greatest living footballers.
Elected UEFA vice-president.

name: Gerben Karstens
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in the 100 km team time trial at the 1964 Tokyo Games at age 22, then turned professional and won Paris-Tours in 1965 and the Dutch national road race championship in 1966.
early_history_summary: Karstens was originally a speed skater at national squad level before choosing cycling. He became Military Champion of the Netherlands in 1962 during national service, finished fifth at the 1963 amateur World Championships, and won Olympic gold in the 1964 team time trial before turning professional in 1965.
family_context_summary: Born in Voorburg, Netherlands. Father was a notary public in Leiden who opposed Karstens' choice of cycling as a career. Middle-class background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a notary public; no family connection to cycling. Father actively opposed Karstens' cycling career choice.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dutch cycling tradition, speed skating background, military sports, Olympic team time trial
evidence_summary: Karstens benefited from the Netherlands' deep cycling culture and his own multi-sport background in speed skating. His father's middle-class profession provided some financial stability, though his father opposed his cycling career, creating a constraint that fueled his determination. National service provided a competitive platform (Military Champion 1962). The Dutch national team system and Olympic team time trial format gave him a path to gold at 22. His sprinting talent was evident early but no elite mentorship is documented.
starting_point: Born in Voorburg, Netherlands to a middle-class family; father was a notary public in Leiden who opposed his cycling career.
current_position: Died October 8, 2022 in Dongen, Netherlands at age 80 after complications from a stroke; remembered as a legendary sprinter with 6 Tour de France and 14 Vuelta a España stage wins.

trajectory.event: Became Military Champion of the Netherlands in cycling during national service.
Won Olympic gold medal in the 100 km team time trial at the Tokyo Games.
Turned professional and won Paris-Tours.
Won Dutch national road race championship and multiple Tour de France stages.
Won a Tour de France stage on the Champs-Élysées and wore the yellow jersey.
Died in Dongen, Netherlands on October 8, 2022 after complications from a stroke.

name: Àlex Corretja
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first ATP Tour singles title at Buenos Aires in 1994 at age 20; by 26 he had won multiple ATP titles, reached the French Open final (1998), won the ATP Tour Championships (1998), and reached a career-high ranking of world No. 2 (1999).
early_history_summary: Born in Barcelona, Corretja won the Orange Bowl under-16 title in 1990 at age 16, turned professional in 1991, and won his first ATP singles title in 1994 at Buenos Aires at age 20. He broke into the top 50 in 1992 and the top 25 in 1994.
family_context_summary: Born in Barcelona, Spain. Family financial background not specifically documented but Barcelona provided access to a strong tennis culture.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Barcelona tennis culture, Spanish tennis system, early junior success, Orange Bowl
evidence_summary: Corretja emerged from Barcelona's strong tennis culture, winning the Orange Bowl under-16 title at 16 and turning professional at 17. The Spanish tennis ecosystem of the early 1990s, with its clay-court specialization and growing pool of talented peers, provided a developmental environment. His first ATP title at 20 in Buenos Aires confirmed his professional trajectory. No specific family advantages, elite mentorship, or financial platform are documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Barcelona, Spain; family background not documented in reviewed sources. Grew in a city with a strong tennis culture.
current_position: Retired from professional tennis in 2005; former world No. 2 and ATP Tour Championships winner; has worked as a tennis commentator and briefly as Spain's Davis Cup captain.

trajectory.event: Won the Orange Bowl under-16 title, gaining attention as a promising junior.
Won his first ATP Tour singles title at Buenos Aires.
Won Italian Open Masters in Rome and broke into the ATP top 10.
Reached French Open final and won the ATP Tour World Championships.
Achieved career-high singles ranking of world No. 2.
Won Indian Wells Masters and helped Spain win its first Davis Cup title.
Retired from professional tennis.

name: Ri Se-gwang
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold medal on vault at the 2006 Asian Games in Doha at age 21, becoming the first North Korean to win vault gold at the Asian Games; won World Championships bronze on vault in 2007 at age 22.
early_history_summary: Ri began gymnastics training at age 7 at the Mangyongdae Children's Palace in Pyongyang. He became active on the international stage from 2003, won East Asian Games bronze on vault in 2005 at age 20, and Asian Games gold on vault in 2006 at age 21.
family_context_summary: Born in South Hamgyong, North Korea. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: North Korean state sports system, Children's Palace training from age 7, vault specialization, international isolation
evidence_summary: Ri's gymnastics career was shaped entirely within North Korea's state sports system, beginning at the Mangyongdae Children's Palace at age 7. The state provided structured training and facilities, identifying and developing him as a vault specialist. His international career began at 18, with Asian Games gold at 21 and World Championship bronze at 22. North Korea's international isolation created both constraints (limited competition access) and a distinctive motivation. He later invented two eponymous vault skills, demonstrating exceptional technical depth.
starting_point: Born in South Hamgyong, North Korea; family background not documented in reviewed sources. Entered the state gymnastics system at age 7 via the Mangyongdae Children's Palace in Pyongyang.
current_position: Retired from gymnastics in February 2020 at age 35; regarded as a hero in North Korea with two eponymous vault skills named in the FIG Code of Points.

trajectory.event: Won bronze medal on vault at the East Asian Games in Macau.
Won gold medal on vault at the Asian Games in Doha, the first North Korean to do so.
Won bronze medal on vault at the World Championships in Stuttgart.
Successfully performed a new vault skill later named the Ri Se Gwang in the FIG Code of Points.
Won World Championships gold on vault in Nanning.
Won Olympic gold medal on vault at the Rio Games.
Announced retirement from gymnastics in February 2020.

name: Srettha Thavisin
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; started career as assistant product manager at Procter & Gamble in 1986 at age 24. Co-founded Sansiri around 1988-1990 (sources conflict on exact year); his major business success came later as CEO. Became Prime Minister of Thailand in 2023 at age 61.
early_history_summary: Born in Bangkok to a family connected to five Thai-Chinese business dynasties. Father died when he was three. Educated in Thailand and the US (University of Massachusetts, Claremont Graduate University). Started career at Procter & Gamble in 1986 before co-founding Sansiri, a real estate company.
family_context_summary: Only child of Captain Amnuay Thavisin and Chodchoy Thavisin; father died when Srettha was three. Family connected to five Thai-Chinese business dynasties (Yip in Tsoi, Chakkapak, Jutrakul, Lamsam, Buranasiri). Mother raised him as a single parent.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family lineage connected to five notable Thai-Chinese business dynasties, providing inherited business networks and social capital in Thailand's commercial elite.
evidence_summary: Srettha's major achievements came well after age 26. While he had strong family business connections and US education, his co-founding of Sansiri is dated to 1988-1990 (sources conflict), and even at the earliest date he was 26 with no prior material milestone. His business prominence and political career (Prime Minister 2023-2024) arrived decades later.

name: Arno Allan Penzias
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; by age 26 he was a graduate student at Columbia University working under Charles Townes. His PhD was completed in 1962 at age 29, and the discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation came in 1964 at age 31. Nobel Prize awarded in 1978.
early_history_summary: Born in Munich to a Jewish family, escaped Nazi Germany via Kindertransport to Britain, then settled in the Bronx, New York in 1940. Graduated from City College of New York in 1954, served in the Army Signal Corps, then enrolled at Columbia University in 1956 to study physics under Charles Townes.
family_context_summary: Born in Munich to Karl and Justine Penzias, who ran a leather business. Jewish family; grandparents were leaders of a Munich synagogue. Family escaped Nazi Germany via Kindertransport, settling in the Bronx, New York in 1940. Grew up as a refugee child in modest circumstances.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no family connection to physics or science.
evidence_summary: Penzias's Nobel Prize-winning discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation occurred in 1964 at age 31, well after age 26. By 26, he was a graduate student at Columbia with no material milestone. His early life was shaped by the adversity of escaping Nazi Germany as a child refugee, but his scientific achievements came through years of graduate training and Bell Labs research positions.
